mainTopic: רבא asks רבה בר מרי for the scriptural sources of many popular sayings, from eating early in the morning to 'like seeks like' and more.
overview: This amud is a long series of questions from רבא to רבה בר מרי. Each time, רבא names a popular saying and asks which פסוק it comes from. It opens with the end of an earlier answer: the מצורע must announce 'Unclean, unclean,' which shows that poverty follows the poor. Next comes the advice to get up early and eat. רבה בר מרי brings a פסוק from ישעיה, and רבא brings one from the תורה: prayer, then bread with salt and water, which removes bile and its 83 illnesses. Many more sayings follow, each matched to a פסוק: accepting the label others give you (הגר), saying your own flaw first (אליעזר), being humble while looking ahead (אביגיל), and the pain of being left out of a meal (נתן, and אברהם marrying קטורה). Others are credit going to the one who pours (משה and יהושע), hunger making bitter things sweet, and like seeking like, which is shown from the תורה, נביאים, כתובים, a משנה and a ברייתא. The amud closes with sayings about giving up on someone who ignores you, not harming a well you drank from, sharing a burden (ברק and דבורה), and being honored when young but treated like a child when old. The answer to that last saying finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: The leper must announce 'Unclean, unclean'
steps.stepSummary: The section opens by finishing an earlier answer. The verse about the מצורע calling out 'Unclean, unclean' is the source for the saying that trouble piles on top of trouble.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And he shall cry: Unclean, unclean."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer that began earlier. It quotes the verse where the מצורע must call out 'Unclean, unclean' as the source for the folk saying that poverty follows the poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצורע already suffers from his disease, and on top of that he must announce it and be embarrassed. That is the picture of one hardship following another, which is the point of the saying.

keyTerms.meaning: A person with the skin disease of צרעת

steps.confusionAlert: This line belongs to the end of the previous question-and-answer. It is not part of the new question about eating in the morning that starts in the next step.

phrases.english: "And he shall cry: Unclean, unclean."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 13:45. This is about the מצורע, who has to announce his own condition. It answers the earlier question about 'poverty follows the poor.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to a question asked before this section begins.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse about the מצורע calling out 'Unclean, unclean' is the source for 'poverty follows the poor.'

steps.title: Where do we learn to eat early in the morning?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רבה בר מרי where the advice of the רבנן to get up early and eat comes from. The advice has a matching folk saying: sixty runners cannot catch the man who ate breakfast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does this teaching of the רבנן come from: 'Get up early and eat, in summer because of the heat and in winter because of the cold'? And people also say: 'Sixty runners ran and could not catch up to the man who ate in the morning.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts a new question in his series. He asks for the verse behind a piece of health advice: eat early in the morning. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advice has two parts. A morning meal protects you from summer heat and from winter cold. The folk saying adds that a person who ate breakfast has more strength than sixty people running on empty. רבא wants to know which verse supports this.

keyTerms.meaning: Where does this teaching come from?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that the Sages said:
Get up early and eat,
in the summer because of the heat,
and in the winter because of the cold;
and people say:
Sixty runners ran,
and they did not reach the man who ate in the morning?
phrases.notes: כְּרַךְ literally means 'wrapped.' Here it means he ate a meal of bread.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה רבא לרבה בר מרי מנא הא מילתא דאמור רבנן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question in רבא's series of requests for sources of sayings.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the advice to eat early in the morning to protect against heat and cold.

steps.title: Answer from ישעיה: they will not hunger and the heat will not strike them
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי answers with a verse from ישעיה. It links not being hungry or thirsty with being protected from heat and sun.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "They shall not hunger nor thirst, and neither heat nor sun shall strike them."
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי gives his source, a verse from ישעיה. It connects not being hungry with not being hurt by the weather.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse puts two ideas side by side: not hungry or thirsty, and not struck by heat or sun. רבה בר מרי reads this as cause and effect. A person who has eaten is protected from the weather, which matches 'get up early and eat because of the heat.'

phrases.english: As it is written: "They shall not hunger nor thirst,
phrases.notes: ישעיה 49:10.

phrases.english: and neither heat nor sun shall strike them."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's question from step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ישעיה 49:10 links not being hungry with protection from heat and sun.

steps.title: רבא's own source from the תורה: bread and water after prayer
steps.stepSummary: רבא offers a different source, a verse in the תורה. He reads 'serve ה׳' as קריאת שמע and תפילה, 'bread and water' as a morning meal of bread with salt and a jug of water, and then 'I will remove sickness.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You bring it from there, and I bring it from here: "And you shall serve ה׳ your God": this is קריאת שמע and תפילה. "And He will bless your bread and your water": this is bread with salt and a jug of water. From then on: "And I will remove sickness from among you."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers that he prefers a verse from the תורה over the verse from ישעיה. He reads the verse as a morning schedule: pray first, then eat bread and water, and as a result sickness goes away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר מרי's verse comes from נביאים. רבא finds the idea in the תורה itself (שמות 23:25). He reads each part of the verse in order: serving ה׳ is the morning קריאת שמע and תפילה, the bread and water is the simple meal right after, and removing sickness is the health benefit.

keyTerms.term: אַתְּ אָמְרַתְּ מֵהָתָם וַאֲנָא אָמֵינָא מֵהָכָא
keyTerms.meaning: You bring it from there, and I bring it from here (a different source)
Reciting שמע and the עמידה prayer

steps.whyThisMatters: This passage is a source for the practice of praying first in the morning and then eating a simple breakfast.

phrases.english: He said to him: You say it from there,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the verse in ישעיה, from נביאים.

phrases.english: and I say it from here:
"And you shall serve the Lord your God":
phrases.notes: שמות 23:25.

phrases.english: this is the recitation of Shema and prayer.
"And He will bless your bread and your water":
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is filled in so the quote matches the פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: זוֹ פַּת בְּמֶלַח וְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל מַיִם.
phrases.english: this is bread with salt and a jug of water.
From here on:
"And I will remove sickness from among you."

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה את אמרת מהתם ואנא אמינא מהכא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second source, from the תורה, in place of the verse from ישעיה in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The advice to eat early in the morning
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 23:25, read as prayer, then bread with salt and water, then removal of sickness.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the 'sickness' is bile, which holds 83 illnesses
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that the 'sickness' in the verse is bile (מרה). Bile holds 83 illnesses, the גימטריא of מחלה, and a morning meal of bread with salt and a jug of water cancels all of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a ברייתא teaches: 'Sickness' means bile. Why is it called 'sickness' (מחלה)? Because it holds eighty-three illnesses, and that is the numerical value of the word מחלה. And all of them are cancelled by bread with salt in the morning and a jug of water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רבא's reading. It names the 'sickness' in the verse and shows how much good the morning meal does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the 'sickness' is bile. It explains the name with גימטריא: מ(40)+ח(8)+ל(30)+ה(5) = 83, the number of illnesses bile can cause. Then it says outright that bread with salt in the morning and a jug of water cancels all 83. That confirms רבא's reading of the verse.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא learns the morning routine from the תורה: קריאת שמע and תפילה, then bread with salt and a jug of water. This removes 'sickness,' meaning bile and its 83 illnesses.

phrases.english: And it is taught: "Sickness": this is bile.
And why is it called "sickness"?
Because it holds eighty-three illnesses:
"Machala" in numerical value comes to that.
phrases.notes: מ is 40, ח is 8, ל is 30, ה is 5. Together they make 83.

phrases.english: And all of them, bread with salt in the morning
and a jug of water cancels them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's reading in step 4 by explaining what the 'sickness' is and confirming that the morning meal removes it.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's reading that the morning bread and water removes sickness
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: מחלה is bile, which has 83 illnesses (the גימטריא of מחלה), and bread with salt and water in the morning cancels them all.

steps.title: Where Is the Source for 'If Your Friend Calls You a Donkey, Put On the Saddle'?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רבה בר מרי for the source of the רבנן's saying that if your friend calls you a donkey, you should put a saddle on your back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where do we learn what the רבנן said, 'If your friend calls you a donkey, put a saddle on your back'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new round of the same question-and-answer game from Step 2. This time he asks for the source of a saying about accepting what others call you, and the next step gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying means you should not argue with how others describe you. Go along with it, as if to say, 'Fine, I'll wear the saddle.' רבא assumes that wise sayings like this have a hint somewhere in the פסוקים, and he wants to find it.

keyTerms.meaning: Put on, place (here: put the saddle on your back)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that the Sages said:
If your friend calls you a 'donkey'
put a saddle on your back?
phrases.notes: Don't fight the label. Just go along with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new round of the same question pattern used in Step 2, now about a new saying.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that hints at the idea of accepting what others call you instead of arguing.

steps.title: הגר Answers to the Title 'Maid of שרי'
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי answers with the פסוק where the מלאך calls הגר 'maid of שרי' and she accepts the title.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written: 'And he said: הגר, maid of שרי, where have you come from and where are you going? And she said: I am running away from שרי my mistress.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי gives the source for the donkey-and-saddle saying. It is the conversation between the מלאך and הגר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this point הגר had run away, so she was no longer acting as שרי's maid. Still, when the מלאך called her 'maid of שרי,' she did not argue. She answered in those same terms and called שרי 'my mistress.' That is the idea of the saying: when someone gives you a title, wear it.

keyTerms.meaning: הגר, the maidservant who ran away from שרי

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"And he said: Hagar, maid of Sarai,
phrases.notes: בראשית 16:8. The 'he' speaking is the מלאך.

phrases.english: where have you come from, and where are you going?

phrases.aramaic: וַתֹּאמֶר: מִפְּנֵי שָׂרַי גְּבִרְתִּי אָנֹכִי בּוֹרַחַת״.
phrases.english: And she said: I am fleeing from Sarai my mistress."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: הגר accepts the label 'maid of שרי' even though she had run away, which shows the idea of accepting what others call you.

steps.title: Where Is the Source for 'Say Your Own Embarrassing Fact First'?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the source of the popular saying that if you have an embarrassing flaw, you should say it before others do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where do we learn what people say, 'An embarrassing thing that is in you, say it first'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks the next question in the series. It is about a saying that tells you to admit your own weak point before someone else brings it up, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Notice the wording has changed. Here the saying comes from ordinary people ('דאמרי אינשי'), not from the רבנן as in Step 6. The advice is practical: if you mention your flaw first, nobody can use it to shame you.

keyTerms.meaning: Be first, go ahead of others

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that people say:
A shameful thing that is in you
say it first?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another round of the same question pattern, now about a new saying.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that hints at the idea of mentioning your own flaw before others do.

steps.title: אליעזר Opens With 'I Am the Servant of אברהם'
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי brings the פסוק where אברהם's servant begins his speech by announcing that he is a servant.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written: 'And he said: I am the servant of אברהם.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers with the first words אליעזר says to רבקה's family when he comes to find a wife for יצחק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being a servant was a lowly position, and the family might have looked down on it. Instead of waiting for them to find out, אליעזר says it right away as his very first words. That is exactly the saying: say your own embarrassing fact first.

keyTerms.meaning: אברהם, the master of the servant speaking

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"And he said: I am Abraham's servant."
phrases.notes: בראשית 24:34.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אליעזר's first words announce that he is a servant, so he states his lowly status before anyone else can.

steps.title: Where Is the Source for 'The Goose Bends Low but Its Eyes Look Far'?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the source of the saying that a goose walks with its head bent low while its eyes search far ahead.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where do we learn what people say, 'The goose walks bent low, but its eyes look far away'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks the next question in the series. This saying is about someone who acts humble but is still watching out for his own future benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A goose walks with its head down, so it looks humble. But its eyes are scanning ahead for food. The picture describes a person who speaks humbly while quietly planning what he will gain later.

keyTerms.meaning: Look far ahead, scan the distance

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that people say:
The goose goes along bent low,
but its eyes look far off?
phrases.notes: It is looking ahead for food, even while its head is down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another round of the same question pattern, now about a new saying.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that hints at someone acting humble while still looking out for future gain.

steps.title: אביגיל Humbly Asks דוד to Remember Her Later
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי brings אביגיל's words to דוד. While pleading humbly, she also asks him to remember her once he succeeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written: 'And when ה׳ does good to my master, then remember your maidservant.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers with what אביגיל said to דוד when she came to ask him to spare נבל her husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביגיל spoke very humbly and called herself 'your maidservant.' At the same moment she was thinking ahead, asking דוד to remember her when he became king. That is the goose: head low, eyes looking far ahead.

keyTerms.meaning: אביגיל, the wife of נבל, who spoke to דוד

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"And when the Lord does good to my lord,
phrases.notes: שמואל א 25:31.

phrases.english: then remember your maidservant."
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is part of the corrected wording of the פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אביגיל speaks humbly to דוד but also asks him to remember her in the future, like the goose that bends low while looking ahead.

steps.title: Where Is the Source for 'Hearing Others Eat Without You Hurts'?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the source of the saying that sixty pains come to the teeth of someone who hears others eating while he does not eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where do we learn what people say, 'Sixty pains reach the teeth of one who hears his friend eating and does not eat'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks the next question in the series. This saying is about how painful it is to be left out of a meal while others enjoy it, and the next step gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying describes the feeling of hearing other people eat while you sit with nothing. 'Sixty' is just a way of saying 'a great many.' The point is how much it hurts to be left out.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that people say:
Sixty pains reach the teeth
of one who hears the sound of his friend eating and does not eat?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another round of the same question pattern, now about a new saying.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that shows the pain of being left out while others eat.

steps.title: נתן Complains That He Was Not Invited to the Feast
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי brings נתן's words to דוד. When אדניה made a feast, he left out נתן, צדוק, בניהו, and שלמה, and the hurt shows in how נתן lists them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written: 'But me, I your servant, and צדוק the כהן, and בניהו son of יהוידע, and שלמה your servant, he did not invite.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers with נתן הנביא telling דוד about אדניה's feast, which he and others were not invited to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נתן lists by name each person who was left out, starting with himself ('me, I your servant'). His careful list shows the sting of hearing about a feast you were not part of. That matches the saying about the pain of hearing others eat. The next step gives רבא's own source from the תורה for this same saying.

keyTerms.meaning: בניהו son of יהוידע, one of דוד's officers
שלמה, דוד's son and future king
He did not invite (literally, 'did not call')

steps.whatToRemember: In this series, רבא names a saying and asks for its source, and רבה בר מרי answers with a פסוק that shows the same idea in action. So far: accept the label others give you (הגר), say your own flaw first (אליעזר), be humble but look ahead (אביגיל), and being left out of a meal hurts (נתן).

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"But me, I your servant, and Zadok the priest,
phrases.notes: מלכים א 1:26. נתן הנביא is speaking to דוד about אדניה's feast.

phrases.english: and Benaiah son of Jehoiada,
and Solomon your servant, he did not invite."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12; רבא adds a second source for the same saying in Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: נתן's pained list of everyone left out of אדניה's feast shows how much it hurts to hear of others eating while you were not included.

steps.title: רבא offers a תורה source for the sixty pains saying
steps.stepSummary: רבא says: you brought a source from נביאים, but I bring one from the תורה. Right after יצחק marries רבקה, the תורה says that אברהם took another wife, קטורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: You brought the proof from there, and I bring it from here. 'And יצחק brought her into the tent of שרה his mother, and he took רבקה and she became his wife, and he loved her, and יצחק was comforted after his mother.' And right after that it is written: 'And אברהם again took a wife, and her name was קטורה.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different, earlier source for the saying from Step 12, about sixty pains for someone who hears others eating while he does not eat. His source is from the תורה instead of נביאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם saw his son happily married while he himself was alone, and that hurt him, like someone watching others eat. The proof is that the תורה tells us right away that אברהם married again. This is not an argument against רבה בר מרי, only an earlier source for the same idea.

keyTerms.meaning: After it, right next to it

steps.confusionAlert: Here it is רבא, the one who usually asks, who gives the answer. He is not rejecting רבה בר מרי's source. He is adding an earlier one from the תורה.

phrases.english: He said to him: You said it from there
phrases.notes: רבא is speaking here. 'There' is the פסוק about נתן and אדניה's feast from Step 13.

phrases.english: and I say it from here:
"And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother,
phrases.notes: בראשית 24:67

phrases.aramaic: וַיִּקַּח אֶת רִבְקָה וַתְּהִי לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה
phrases.english: and he took Rebekah and she became his wife
and he loved her, and Isaac was comforted after his mother,"
and it is written right after it:
"And Abraham again took a wife,
phrases.notes: בראשית 25:1

phrases.english: and her name was Keturah."

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתְּ אָמְרַתְּ מֵהָתָם, וַאֲנָא אָמֵינָא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative, earlier source for the saying answered in Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for 'sixty pains come to one who hears others eating' (from Step 12).
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The order of the פסוקים: יצחק marries רבקה, and right after, אברהם marries קטורה.

steps.title: Source for credit going to the one who pours the wine
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the source of the saying: the wine belongs to its owner, but the thanks go to the one who pours it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does the saying people use come from, 'The wine belongs to its owner, but the thanks go to the one who pours it'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks about a new folk saying. A host may own the wine, but the guests thank the waiter who pours it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of the saying is that the person who hands over a gift often gets the credit, even if the gift is not really his. רבא wants a פסוק that shows this same idea.

keyTerms.meaning: Where does this saying that people say come from?
The one who pours it, the server

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that people say:
The wine belongs to its owner,
but the thanks go to the one who pours it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next folk saying in the series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק showing that the one who passes something along gets the credit for it.

steps.title: משה laying hands on יהושע gets the credit
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי brings the פסוקים about משה laying his hands on יהושע. The wisdom came from ה׳, but the תורה says יהושע was full of wisdom because משה laid his hands on him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written: 'And you shall lay your hand upon him... so that all the congregation of the children of ישראל may listen and see.' And it is written: 'And יהושע the son of נון was full of the spirit of wisdom, because משה had laid his hands upon him, and all the children of ישראל listened to him...'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers with two פסוקים about משה passing his leadership to יהושע by placing his hands on him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirit of wisdom really came from ה׳, the 'owner of the wine.' Still, the פסוק credits it to משה, who 'poured' it by laying his hands on יהושע. That matches the saying exactly.

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"And you shall lay your hand upon him"
phrases.notes: במדבר 27:18

phrases.aramaic: – ״לְמַעַן יִשְׁמְעוּן וְיִרְאוּן כׇּל עֲדַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״.
phrases.english: "so that all the congregation of the children of Israel may listen and see."

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב: ״וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן מָלֵא רוּחַ חׇכְמָה,
phrases.english: And it is written: "And Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom,
phrases.notes: דברים 34:9

phrases.aramaic: כִּי סָמַךְ מֹשֶׁה אֶת יָדָיו עָלָיו,
phrases.english: because Moses had laid his hands upon him,

phrases.aramaic: וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ אֵלָיו כׇּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: and all the children of Israel listened to him, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wisdom from ה׳ is credited to משה, who laid his hands on יהושע.

steps.title: Source for a hungry dog eating dung
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the source of the saying that a hungry dog will even swallow dung.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does the saying people use come from, 'A dog in its hunger swallows dung'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks about another folk saying. When you are desperate enough, even disgusting things seem good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying teaches that hunger changes how a person sees things. רבא wants a פסוק that shows the same idea.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that people say:
A dog in its hunger swallows dung?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the letter מ in round brackets and some leave it out. Either way, it means 'swallows.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next folk saying in the series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק showing that hunger makes even bad things acceptable.

steps.title: A hungry soul finds even bitter things sweet
steps.stepSummary: The source is a פסוק in משלי: a full person turns away from honey, but to a hungry person every bitter thing is sweet.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'A full soul tramples a honeycomb, but to a hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet.'
steps.whatsHappening: The answer comes right away from a פסוק in משלי that says the same thing as the dog saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who is full rejects even honey. Someone who is starving accepts even bitter food. This is exactly the dog eating dung.

phrases.english: As it is written:
"A full soul tramples a honeycomb,
phrases.notes: משלי 27:7

phrases.english: but to a hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משלי 27:7: to the hungry, every bitter thing is sweet.

steps.title: Source for a bad palm tree joining barren trees
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the source of the saying that a bad palm tree goes off to stand among barren trees. In other words, bad people look for bad company.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does the saying people use come from, 'A bad palm tree strolls over to a grove of barren trees'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks about one more folk saying, about bad things being drawn to their own kind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The picture is a fruitless palm tree that ends up among other trees that give no fruit. It means that bad people are drawn to other bad people.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that people say:
A bad palm tree strolls and goes
over to a grove of barren trees?
phrases.notes: Bad people seek out other bad people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next folk saying in the series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that like is drawn to like, especially among bad people.

steps.title: This idea appears everywhere in the תורה tradition
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי says this idea is written in the תורה, repeated in נביאים, written a third time in כתובים, and also taught in a משנה and in a ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This matter is written in the תורה, repeated in נביאים, and mentioned a third time in כתובים. And we learned it in a משנה, and we learned it in a ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי begins his answer by saying this idea shows up in five places. This line sets up the list of actual sources, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the earlier sayings, which had one or two פסוקים, this idea is supported by every part of תנ״ך and by תורה שבעל פה as well. This shows how strong and widespread the idea is. The next two steps quote the specific sources.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דָּבָר זֶה כָּתוּב בַּתּוֹרָה,
phrases.english: He said to him: This matter is written in the Torah,
phrases.notes: He only lists the places here. The actual sources come right after this.

phrases.english: repeated in the Prophets,
and mentioned a third time in the Writings;
and we learned it in a mishna,
and we learned it in a baraita.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר זֶה כָּתוּב בַּתּוֹרָה, שָׁנוּי בַּנְּבִיאִים, וּמְשׁוּלָּשׁ בַּכְּתוּבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering Step 19 by listing where the sources are found.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The idea appears in the תורה, נביאים, כתובים, a משנה, and a ברייתא. The details follow.

steps.title: Three פסוקים showing that like goes to like
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי gives the פסוק from the תורה (עשו went to ישמעאל), from נביאים (empty men gathered to יפתח), and from כתובים (every bird lives with its kind).
steps.simpleTranslation: In the תורה: 'עשו went to ישמעאל.' In נביאים: 'Empty men gathered to יפתח and were with him.' In כתובים: 'Every bird dwells with its kind, and a person with someone like him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי now fills in the details of his answer from Step 20 and names the actual פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each פסוק shows people who are alike joining together. עשו, who was not a good person, went to ישמעאל. Empty, worthless men gathered around יפתח. The third source says this directly about birds and people.

keyTerms.meaning: Repeated in the נביאים (the second time it shows up)
Said a third time, in the כתובים
To someone who is like him

phrases.english: It is written in the Torah, as it is written:
"And Esau went to Ishmael."
phrases.notes: בראשית 28:9

phrases.english: It is repeated in the Prophets, as it is written:
"And empty men gathered to Yiftach,
and they were with him."
phrases.notes: שופטים 11:3

phrases.english: And it is said a third time in the Writings, as it is written:
"Every bird dwells with its own kind,
and a person with one who is like him."
phrases.notes: This line comes from ספר בן סירא. Some versions say 'people', the word in round brackets. The word in square brackets is the corrected wording, 'a person.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the details of the three-part answer promised in Step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: פסוקים about עשו, יפתח, and birds of a kind show that like seeks out like.

steps.title: A משנה and a ברייתא with the same idea
steps.stepSummary: The same idea shows up in a משנה about טומאה (what is attached takes on the status of what it is attached to) and in a ברייתא from רבי אליעזר about a starling and a raven.
steps.simpleTranslation: A משנה teaches: whatever is attached to something impure is impure, and whatever is attached to something pure is pure. A ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר says the starling did not go to the raven for no reason. It went because it is the same kind.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי finishes his list with the fourth and fifth sources: a משנה and a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is about the laws of טומאה, but it carries the same lesson: what you attach yourself to decides what you become. רבי אליעזר's bird example shows that creatures that are alike, here two non-kosher birds, end up together.

keyTerms.meaning: Not for nothing; there is a reason

steps.whatToRemember: The idea that people are drawn to others like them is found in all five places: תורה, נביאים, כתובים, משנה, and ברייתא.

phrases.english: We learned it in a Mishnah:
phrases.notes: כלים 12:2

phrases.english: Anything attached to something impure is impure;
anything attached to something pure is pure.
And we learned it in a baraita:
Rabbi Eliezer says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא לְחִנָּם הָלַךְ זַרְזִיר אֵצֶל עוֹרֵב,
phrases.english: Not for nothing did the starling go to the raven,
but because it is its kind.
phrases.notes: Both of these birds are non-kosher, so they count as the same kind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the five-part answer by adding the משנה and the ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה about attachment and טומאה, and רבי אליעזר's ברייתא about the starling and the raven.

steps.title: Source for giving up on someone who ignores you
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks where the saying comes from: if you called your friend and he didn't answer, knock a big wall over on him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does this saying come from: 'You called your friend and he didn't answer you, push over a big wall onto him'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new question in the same series and asks for the source of another folk saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying means that if you reached out to help someone and he ignored you, you can stop trying to help him. רבא wants to know which פסוק teaches this.

keyTerms.meaning: Where does this thing come from?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this thing that people say:
"You called your friend and he did not answer you,
push over a big wall and throw it at him"?
phrases.notes: Stop trying to help someone who won't respond to you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the same series of folk-saying questions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק behind giving up on someone who ignores your call.

steps.title: The source in יחזקאל
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי answers from יחזקאל: because I purified you and you did not become pure, you will not be purified anymore.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: 'Because I purified you and you did not become pure from your impurity, you will not become pure anymore.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers רבא with a פסוק from יחזקאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ tried to purify the people and they did not respond, so He says He will stop trying. That matches the saying: once you reach out and are ignored, you may stop.

keyTerms.meaning: You will not become pure anymore

phrases.english: He said to him:
"Because I purified you and you did not become pure from your impurity,
you will not become pure anymore."
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 24:13

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יחזקאל 24:13: ה׳ stops purifying those who did not respond.

steps.title: Source for not harming a well you drank from
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks where the saying comes from: don't throw a stone into a well you drank from.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does this saying come from: 'A well that you drank from, don't throw a stone into it'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks about another folk saying in the same series.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying means you should not harm a person or place that once helped you. רבא wants the פסוק that teaches this kind of gratitude.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, a stone or clod of earth

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this thing that people say:
"A well that you drank from,
do not throw a stone into it"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the same series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק behind not harming someone who helped you.

steps.title: The source: do not despise the מצרי
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי answers from דברים: do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother; do not despise an Egyptian, for you lived in his land.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: As it is written, 'Do not despise an Edomite, because he is your brother. Do not despise an Egyptian, because you were a stranger in his land.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers with a פסוק from the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though מצרים later made בני ישראל suffer, they first gave בני ישראל a place to live. So the תורה says not to despise them. In the same way, you should not harm a 'well' you once drank from.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not despise or treat as disgusting
An Edomite, a descendant of עשו

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother;

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא תְתַעֵב מִצְרִי – כִּי גֵר הָיִיתָ בְאַרְצוֹ״.
phrases.english: and do not despise an Egyptian, for you were a stranger in his land."
phrases.notes: דברים 23:8. The part about the Egyptian is the main proof here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דברים 23:8: do not despise the מצרי, because you lived in his land.

steps.title: Source for 'I'll lift only if you lift too'
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks where the saying comes from: if you lift the load with me, I'll lift; if not, I won't.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does this saying come from: 'If you lift the load, I'll lift; and if not, I won't lift'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks about one more folk saying in the series.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying is about a partnership: I will do my share only if you do yours. רבא wants the פסוק that shows this.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this thing that people say:
"If you lift the load, I will lift;
and if not, I will not lift"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the same series.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק behind joining a task only if the other person joins too.

steps.title: The source: ברק and דבורה
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי answers from שופטים: ברק told דבורה he would go to war only if she went with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: As it is written, 'ברק said to her: If you go with me, I will go; and if you do not go with me, I will not go.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי answers with ברק's words to דבורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ברק made his part depend on דבורה doing her part, exactly like the saying 'I'll lift only if you lift.'

keyTerms.meaning: The army leader in the days of דבורה

steps.whatToRemember: Each of רבא's folk sayings is matched to a פסוק: ignored help (יחזקאל), gratitude to a 'well' (the מצרי in דברים), and shared burdens (ברק and דבורה).

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"And Barak said to her:
phrases.notes: 'Her' is דבורה.

phrases.english: If you go with me, then I will go;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לֹא תֵלְכִי עִמִּי – לֹא אֵלֵךְ״.
phrases.english: and if you do not go with me, I will not go."
phrases.notes: שופטים 4:8

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שופטים 4:8: ברק will go only if דבורה goes with him.

steps.title: רבא asks the source for: young we were men, old we are children
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רבה בר מרי for a פסוק behind the saying that people were treated as grown men when young, but as children now that they are old.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where does this saying come from that people say: 'When we were young, we were treated like men; now that I am old, I am treated like a child'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks another question in his series, looking for a פסוק that matches a well-known folk saying. This sets up רבה בר מרי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying describes a strange reversal: normally a person gains respect as he gets older, but here he loses it. רבא wants a source in תנ״ך that shows this same pattern of honor going down over time.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari
From where is this matter derived
that people say
When we were young, we were treated as men
phrases.notes: The words 'we were treated' aren't written. The saying just says 'to men,' meaning people related to us like adults.

phrases.english: now that I am old, as children?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another question in the same series of רבא asking for sources of popular sayings
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק showing that someone is treated with more importance early on and less importance later

steps.title: At first God Himself led Israel in the desert
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי begins his answer: at first the פסוק says ה׳ Himself went before the Jewish people in a pillar of cloud and fire, but at the end a different פסוק is written.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: At first it is written: 'And ה׳ went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light.' And at the end it is written:
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי starts answering by quoting a פסוק from שמות showing that in the beginning ה׳ Himself led the Jewish people. He then sets up a contrast with a later פסוק, which comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half of the proof shows the 'young' stage: right after leaving מצרים, the people got the highest honor, being led by ה׳ directly. The words 'at the end it is written' tell us a second פסוק will show a lower level of honor later on, matching the saying.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer isn't finished here. The contrasting פסוק after 'at the end it is written' comes at the start of the next amud, so don't treat the first פסוק alone as the full proof.

phrases.english: He said to him
At first it is written
"And the Lord went before them by day
in a pillar of cloud, to lead them the way
and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light"
phrases.notes: שמות 13:21

phrases.english: And at the end it is written:
phrases.notes: The second פסוק comes at the start of the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29 by starting a contrast between two פסוקים
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: At first ה׳ Himself led the Jewish people with pillars of cloud and fire (the 'young' stage of honor), to be contrasted with a later פסוק showing less honor
